prompt_free_text:
This paper studies general upper and lower bounds on the KL error of Bayesian coreset posteriors. The main message is appealing and important: existing theory for Bayesian coresets is either narrow or heavily assumption-laden, whereas practical coreset methods are used in models that are multimodal, weakly identifiable, or heavy-tailed. The paper aims to close this gap by proving lower bounds under relatively mild local asymptotic assumptions and upper bounds under a generalized subexponentiality condition, then using these results to explain why importance-weighted coresets can fail and why subsample-optimize methods can succeed.

Overall, I find the paper technically ambitious, conceptually valuable, and potentially impactful. The strongest contribution is the lower-bound perspective. The field has many positive results and empirical demonstrations, but relatively little theory explaining when coreset approximations fundamentally cannot work well. The paper’s negative results for importance-weighted constructions are especially useful: they formalize an intuition many practitioners have observed empirically, namely that unbiasedness of the surrogate log-likelihood is far from sufficient for posterior accuracy. The upper-bound side is also interesting, particularly because it is framed in terms of a covariance/subexponential control on centered log-likelihoods rather than strong log-concavity or exponential-family structure.

I think the paper is likely publishable if the proofs are correct, but I also think the presentation and some claims need sharpening. My main concerns are about the practical interpretability of the assumptions, the strength and novelty of the upper-bound application, and some ambiguity in how “general” the results really are.

The lower-bound framework in Section 3 is the highlight. Lemma 3.1 appears to be a useful generic reduction from KL to a localized overlap quantity. The subsequent theorems then leverage local posterior concentration around a point theta_0 and compare the normalized gradients g/N and g_w / sum_n w_n. This is a clever reduction because it turns posterior approximation analysis into a weighted random-vector approximation problem. That is a meaningful conceptual advance. In particular, the distinction between Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.5 is sensible: one theorem handles the regime where the coreset is “almost good” but not good enough, while the other handles more severe mismatch under a weak global lower-smoothness condition.

The applications of these lower bounds are compelling. Corollaries 4.1 and 4.2 give a strong and memorable conclusion: importance-weighted coresets require M proportional to N to keep KL bounded, and even optimal post-hoc scaling only improves the lower bound from N/M to log(N/M). This is a valuable negative result because importance weighting is a natural baseline and often the first thing one tries. Corollary 4.3 is also interesting as a dimension-dependent impossibility statement for arbitrary coreset constructions with M < d. These results together give the paper a strong identity.

That said, I would like the authors to be more careful in how broadly they phrase these impossibility conclusions. The lower bounds are asymptotic and depend on concentration around a local parameterization, moment assumptions, and specific regularity conditions. The paper often says these assumptions are “mild” or “typical,” which may be true relative to prior coreset theory, but the conclusions are still not fully model-agnostic. For example, the lower-bound applications in Section 4 rely on i.i.d. sampling, Fisher-type identities, finite moments of gradients/Hessians, and concentration rates. These are standard in asymptotic statistics, but they exclude some settings where coresets are used. I would encourage the authors to distinguish more explicitly between “general relative to prior coreset theory” and “general across Bayesian models.”

The upper-bound side is somewhat less convincing to me than the lower-bound side. Lemma 5.1 is elegant, and Theorem 5.3 gives a clean KL control from a multivariate subexponential condition. However, Definition 5.2 is abstract, and Proposition 5.4 only states existence of some beta under local finiteness of exponential moments around the origin. This makes the result mathematically broad but somewhat operationally weak. In practice, to use the theorem one needs either a computable A and f or at least interpretable sufficient conditions implying a reasonable beta. The conclusion in Section 7 acknowledges this limitation, but it is central enough that it weakens the practical force of the upper-bound theory.

Relatedly, Corollary 6.1 for subsample-optimize methods is interesting but rests on an alignment condition in Equation 27 that feels difficult to verify and potentially close to encoding the desired success of the algorithm. The statement is still useful as a conditional theorem, but I do not think it fully explains why subsample-optimize methods work in broad practice unless the alignment probability can be related to more primitive properties of the model or sampling distribution. As written, the lower-bound applications feel more definitive than the upper-bound applications. I would recommend the authors frame the upper-bound contribution more modestly: it provides a flexible route to proving bounded KL for subsample-optimize methods, but not yet a turnkey theorem for broad classes of models.

The empirical section is directionally supportive but limited. It is good that the experiments focus on models violating standard assumptions: the multimodal/unidentifiable Cauchy location model and the heavy-tailed unidentifiable logistic regression model are appropriate stress tests. The plots seem to support the predicted asymptotic rates for importance-weighted methods and bounded behavior for subsample-optimize methods with logarithmic coreset size. However, the empirical scope is narrow. There are only two synthetic examples, and the optimization in Algorithm 3 is implemented via discretized nonnegative least squares rather than exact KL minimization. That is understandable, but it creates a gap between theorem and experiment. Also, the abstract and opening text mention “image data” and “specific applications such as image data,” but the provided paper content does not include image experiments. This inconsistency is distracting and should be fixed.

I also found the exposition uneven in places. The paper is clearly written at a high technical level, but some sections are harder to parse than necessary. The notation around the total coreset weight is garbled in the provided text, likely due to rendering issues, but even aside from that, the dependence of the lower bounds on the various asymptotic regimes could be explained more intuitively. For example, the role of the neighborhood radius r, the term -log pi(B^c), and the transition between local Gaussian approximation and global tail control deserve more discussion. Similarly, the generalized subexponentiality definition would benefit from examples in the main text, not only appendices or propositions. A reader should come away understanding when to expect A-subexponentiality and how it compares concretely to prior assumptions like strong log-concavity.

A few more specific issues merit attention. First, the paper defines coreset quality using the minimum or maximum of forward and reverse KL depending on the theorem. This is reasonable, but the switching between underline-KL and overline-KL can obscure interpretation. It would help to explain more explicitly why lower bounds are stated for the minimum of the two KLs and upper bounds for the maximum, and whether this mismatch leaves a gap in understanding practical posterior approximation quality. Second, Algorithm 3 assumes access to the exact KL minimizer over a sampled support, which is generally intractable. Since the empirical implementation uses a surrogate optimization, the paper should discuss whether the theory extends to approximate optimization error. Third, the computational desiderata in Section 2 include sublinear or near-linear construction cost, but the optimization step in subsample-optimize methods may be nontrivial depending on how posterior expectations are approximated. The practical cost model should be discussed more honestly.

In terms of novelty, I view the paper as making a substantial contribution. The lower bounds, especially for importance-weighted constructions, are the most novel and impactful part. The upper bounds are less sharp in practical terms but still broaden the theoretical toolkit. The combination of negative and positive results is a strength: the paper does not merely propose another method, but clarifies the landscape of what is and is not possible.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, tighten the claims of generality and clearly separate unconditional results from conditional ones. Second, improve the discussion of assumptions, especially for Definition 5.2, Proposition 5.4, and Equation 27, with concrete examples and guidance on verification. Third, reconcile the abstract/introduction with the actual experiments; if image-data claims are not supported here, remove them. Fourth, discuss approximate optimization for Algorithm 3 and how sensitive the upper-bound conclusions are to optimization error. Fifth, expand the empirical section if possible, either with one more realistic benchmark or with ablations showing the effect of sampling probabilities and optimization quality.

To summarize my assessment: this is a strong theory paper with meaningful negative results and a promising general framework. Its main weakness is that the upper-bound side remains somewhat abstract and conditional, and the empirical validation is modest relative to the breadth of the claims. Still, the lower-bound contributions alone are significant enough that I view the paper positively.

My recommendation is accept, leaning weak accept if proof details are fully correct, with the caveat that the final version should sharpen claims, improve exposition, and resolve the inconsistencies in the experimental narrative.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper develops general asymptotic lower and upper bounds on the KL divergence between a full Bayesian posterior and its coreset approximation. The main lower-bound results relate coreset error to mismatch in local gradient/Hessian behavior near a concentration point, under assumptions resembling standard Bayesian asymptotics rather than strong log-concavity or exponential-family structure. These bounds are then used to show that importance-weighted subsampling coresets generally require coreset size proportional to dataset size to keep KL bounded, and that any coreset with fewer than d support points cannot maintain bounded KL when the local likelihood geometry is d-dimensional. On the upper-bound side, the paper introduces a generalized subexponentiality condition on centered log-likelihoods and derives KL upper bounds in terms of a quadratic form in the weight error. This is applied to subsample-optimize methods, yielding bounded asymptotic KL for polylogarithmic coreset sizes under an alignment condition. Empirical illustrations on two synthetic, nonstandard Bayesian models (multimodal/unidentifiable/heavy-tailed) qualitatively support the theoretical claims.
strengths: Addresses an important gap in Bayesian coreset theory by providing both lower and upper KL bounds in settings beyond exponential families and strongly log-concave models.
The lower-bound results are conceptually strong and practically relevant: they explain why simple importance-weighted coresets can fail badly and formalize minimum-size limitations.
Assumptions for the lower bounds are relatively mild and aligned with standard local asymptotic arguments, making the results broadly interesting.
The upper-bound framework via generalized subexponentiality is flexible and potentially applicable to a wide range of models, including heavy-tailed and nonidentifiable examples.
The paper connects abstract theory to concrete algorithmic consequences for importance-weighted and subsample-optimize constructions.
Empirical examples are chosen to stress-test prior theory by using multimodal, unidentifiable, and heavy-tailed posteriors rather than easy log-concave cases.
The distinction between lower bounds for arbitrary constructions and upper bounds for specific constructive methods gives a balanced theoretical picture.
weaknesses: Several key assumptions behind the strongest positive result for subsample-optimize coresets are difficult to verify in practice, especially the alignment probability condition in Eq. 27 and the subexponential constant in Proposition 5.4.

The empirical section is limited to two synthetic examples and mainly provides qualitative confirmation; it does not thoroughly test the sharpness, robustness, or practical relevance of the constants in the bounds.

The optimization step in Algorithm 3 assumes access to the KL-optimal weights over the sampled support, which is generally intractable; the experiments instead use a surrogate optimization, weakening the direct empirical validation of the theorem.
The presentation suggests broad applicability, but some conclusions are asymptotic and local, so their finite-sample implications may be less clear than the narrative implies.

The upper-bound theory is less constructive than the lower-bound theory because the main assumptions needed for bounded KL remain model- and algorithm-dependent and are not reduced to easily checkable generic conditions.
methodological_flaws: There is a notable theory-to-experiment mismatch for Algorithm 3: Corollary 6.1 analyzes weights obtained by exact constrained KL minimization, but the experiments use nonnegative least squares on discretized log-likelihoods. This does not invalidate the theorem, but it weakens the empirical claim that the experiments validate the stated upper-bound result.

Proposition 5.4 is existential: it guarantees some beta yielding subexponentiality if local exponential moments exist, but without quantitative control on beta the resulting upper bound may be too loose to be operational. This limits empirical falsifiability of the positive theory.

The lower-bound applications rely on asymptotic concentration around a point theta_0 and local quadratic structure. For multimodal or weakly identifiable posteriors, this logic can be delicate; although the paper discusses pushforwards and local dependence through eta, the practical scope of the asymptotic approximation in genuinely multimodal settings is not fully clarified.

The claim that the assumptions are 'mild' is somewhat overstated for the upper-bound side: requiring finite exponential moments of centered log-likelihood combinations under the posterior can fail in heavy-tailed settings, and the paper does not fully delineate when this happens versus when Proposition 5.4 applies.

Empirical validity is somewhat narrow: only synthetic models are used, and there is no direct measurement of whether the theorem-specific assumptions (e.g., alignment probability, subexponential behavior) hold empirically in those experiments.
